clue.text: After a little time flower-girl looks bad-tempered

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a short while
Rose is both a flower and a girl's name

explanation.surface: A flower-seller turns sulky after waiting around for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'After' as placing the time first: the girl comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sullen and gloomy in temper is described as morose, a close synonym.

clue.text: One gets fed up with him

blocks.note: surface reading: someone exasperated by a companion

blocks.clueFragment: One gets fed up with him
blocks.note: setter's reading: a companion who is served meals alongside you at the same table on board ship

explanation.surface: Someone who has grown weary of a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' reads as bored, but here it is literal: served food together.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipmate or soldier who eats at the same table in the dining hall.

clue.text: This soldier should feel at home in the orderly room

blocks.note: surface reading: the company office in a barracks

blocks.clueFragment: This soldier should feel at home in the orderly room
blocks.note: setter's reading: orderly is a synonym of the soldier's adjective, steady and methodical

explanation.surface: A soldier who ought to be comfortable in the barracks office.
explanation.walkthrough: An orderly room is a military office; read orderly as an adjective instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A professional, permanent soldier of a standing army, as opposed to a reservist.

clue.text: Might one be seen on a white horse?

definitions.text: Might one be seen on a white horse?

blocks.note: surface reading: a rider on a pale mount

blocks.clueFragment: Might one be seen on a white horse?
blocks.note: setter's reading: white horses are breaking wave crests

explanation.surface: Asking who might be spotted riding a white horse.
explanation.walkthrough: White horses are foam-topped waves, which board enthusiasts ride.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rides breaking waves on a board, a surfer, is literally a rider of foam crests.

clue.text: Where to look for pop records?

definitions.text: Where to look for pop records?

blocks.note: surface reading: a record shop selling chart music

blocks.clueFragment: Where to look for pop records?
blocks.note: setter's reading: pop is British slang for pawn, and the records are the pledge tickets a pawnbroker keeps

explanation.surface: Someone asks where to find a shop selling pop music records.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang to pop something is to pawn it, so the records are of goods pledged, not vinyl discs.
explanation.definitionFit: A pawnbroker's premises keeps a ledger of every item pledged against a loan.

clue.text: King not subject of the idylls but might describe their writer

blocks.clueFragment: King not subject of the idylls
blocks.note: surface reading: Tennyson's Idylls of the King are about Arthur, so this monarch is a different one
setter's reading: the poet's first name was the same as this king's, and he too was great

explanation.surface: A literary note distinguishing a famous monarch from Tennyson's Arthur.
explanation.walkthrough: The Idylls of the King are Tennyson's Arthurian poems; the poet's first name was Alfred.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth-century ruler of Wessex who fought the Danes is the only English monarch called great.

clue.text: A vine trained in simple form

indicators.note: a trained plant is bent into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grape plant trained along a wall into a plain shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsophisticated and innocent, lacking worldly guile, artless in manner.

clue.text: Not quite eighteen inches of rope

indicators.note: not quite means falling a little short, so a letter goes missing from the first half of the measure

blocks.note: a yard is thirty-six inches, so eighteen is half of it

explanation.surface: A length of rope a little under eighteen inches.
explanation.walkthrough: Not quite half is HAL, the half short of its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, a line used for hoisting sails or flags up a mast is a type of rope.

clue.text: Show of force, occasionally

blocks.note: surface reading: an occasional display of military might
setter's reading: a powerful dressage move in which a horse rears on its hind legs, performed now and then at exhibitions

explanation.surface: A periodic demonstration of military power.
explanation.walkthrough: A show here is a horse show, and the display of force is the animal's rearing.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical horsemanship, the horse raises its forelegs and balances on its haunches, a display of strength.

clue.text: Noble flower people

blocks.note: surface reading: the flower of the nobility, its finest members
setter's reading: titled men and women are noble people, and their collective name is also a country name for the wild arum plant

explanation.surface: The cream of the aristocracy.
explanation.walkthrough: The wild arum, or cuckoo-pint, has the folk name lords-and-ladies.
explanation.definitionFit: Peers and their wives are titled nobility, and the phrase is also the folk name of a woodland plant.

clue.text: Hill demonstrates dolce far niente. - -

blocks.note: dolce is Italian for sweet, and sugar is sweetness itself
dolce far niente is Italian for pleasant idleness; far niente, doing nothing, is to loaf

explanation.surface: A lazy hillside scene shows the Italian ideal of sweet idleness.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian phrase is split in two, each half translated; the trailing dots carry the idea on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A conical peak resembling the old moulded block of refined sugar is called by this name, as with Rio's famous mountain.

clue.text: ... as does Dr Johnson in his contributions

blocks.note: surface reading, running on from the clue before: the hill loafs about, and so does Johnson
setter's reading: Johnson wrote a series of essays titled The Idler, so in them he is literally idling

explanation.surface: Following the lazy hill, the great lexicographer is shown lounging too.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues the previous one, so 'as does' stands for loafs; Samuel Johnson's weekly essays of 1758-60 were called The Idler.
explanation.definitionFit: To loaf about doing nothing is to laze, and the third-person verb matches 'does'.

clue.text: She's in the pink

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman in excellent health
setter's reading: pink is a gentle shade of red, and a woman's name spells out that pale colour

explanation.surface: A woman is in fine health and spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the pink' is an idiom for healthy, but here the name is made of a mild red, which is what pink is.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name stands for 'She', and MILD plus RED describes the colour pink.

clue.text: Mere lad appears uncommonly green

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests something out of the usual order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A mere boy looks unusually inexperienced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' tempts as naive, matching the young lad; it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A vivid bright shade of the colour, named after the precious gemstone.

clue.text: Dressed for fatigue duty?

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for attired, clothed in a tire or headdress
second meaning: weary, exhausted, as fatigue suggests

explanation.surface: Soldiers kitted out for menial fatigue duties.
explanation.walkthrough: Fatigues are military chores, but here fatigue simply means weariness; the archaic verb tire meant to dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhausted people suffer weariness, and in older English to tire was to attire, so clothed works too.

clue.text: What some people get up to!

definitions.text: What some people get up to!

blocks.note: surface reading: the mischief people get into

blocks.clueFragment: What some people get up to!
blocks.note: setter's reading: the height climbers or aviators rise to

explanation.surface: A tut-tutting remark about people's goings-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get up to' usually means misbehave; read literally it means climb to a height.
explanation.definitionFit: Height above sea level or ground is what a climber or pilot reaches.

clue.text: He certainly has a voice in civic matters

definitions.text: He certainly has a voice in civic matters

blocks.clueFragment: has a voice in civic matters
blocks.note: surface reading: an influential councillor with a say in local affairs

blocks.clueFragment: He certainly has a voice in civic matters
blocks.note: setter's reading: an official who loudly calls out public announcements in the streets

explanation.surface: A local figure with real influence in council business.
explanation.walkthrough: Having a voice usually means having a say; here it is literal loudness.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional municipal official who rang a bell and shouted proclamations in public places.

clue.text: Rest play this instrument with variations

indicators.note: variations are musical reworkings of a theme, so the letters are reworked into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A musician told to rest and then play a piece with variations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' reads as a musical pause, but it is simply part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ancient stringed device plucked like a zither, used for accompanying psalms.

clue.text: Do time-servers get fed up with this?

definitions.text: Do time-servers get fed up with this?

blocks.note: surface reading: idlers or prisoners growing weary of something

blocks.clueFragment: Do time-servers get fed up with this?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the oat breakfast is food served up, and in British slang it also means a prison sentence

explanation.surface: Wondering whether prisoners tire of their dreary routine.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang doing porridge means serving a prison term, so prisoners both serve it and are fed it.
explanation.definitionFit: An oatmeal breakfast dish, and by slang extension a stretch of time in jail.

clue.text: But it's enjoyed out of doors even in the close season

definitions.text: But it's enjoyed out of doors even in the close season

blocks.note: surface reading: the period when hunting or fishing is banned

blocks.clueFragment: But it's enjoyed out of doors even in the close season
blocks.note: setter's reading: close also means stuffy, its opposite being the fresh outdoor atmosphere

explanation.surface: Some outdoor pleasure still allowed when the sporting season is shut.
explanation.walkthrough: The close season is when game may not be taken; close weather is muggy, and open is close's opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Outdoors, outside rather than indoors, the fresh atmosphere beyond walls.

clue.text: Sticks in a worthless part of London

indicators.note: read as worth-less, it says the place is lacking the word worth

blocks.note: Wandsworth is a borough of south-west London

explanation.surface: Something lodged in a run-down district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worthless' splits as worth-less: take WORTH away from the borough.
explanation.definitionFit: Magicians and conductors use slender rods, which are thin sticks.

clue.text: All bent on a change of game

indicators.note: a change means a fresh arrangement, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Everyone determined to switch to another sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A team sport, similar to basketball, played mainly by women and girls in Britain.

clue.text: Drink may so damage one?

blocks.note: first meaning: whisky distilled in Scotland
second meaning: to wound or cut

explanation.surface: Wondering whether whisky might harm a person.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb to scotch means to wound slightly or put an end to.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisky is the spirit from Scotland, and to injure by gashing is the old verb sense.

clue.text: This team is after a win in Sussex

indicators.note: what lies after the letters of win is what is kept, so those opening letters are dropped from the place

blocks.note: Winchelsea is a small historic town in East Sussex, standing for the place the clue points to

explanation.surface: A football team chasing a victory down in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a club hungry for victory; really the club is what follows WIN in the name of a Sussex town.
explanation.definitionFit: A London football club, playing at Stamford Bridge, is a well-known sporting team.

clue.text: Frankly this law Henry V disputed

blocks.note: surface reading: speaking candidly

blocks.clueFragment: Frankly this law Henry V disputed
blocks.note: setter's reading: the code came from the Salian Franks, and Shakespeare's Henry V debates whether it bars his claim to France

explanation.surface: An honest remark that the king challenged a law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frankly' means 'in the manner of the Franks': the law barring inheritance through women came from them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Frankish code excluding females from succession, cited by the French against Henry's claim.

clue.text: Article remodelled in telling fashion

indicators.note: remodelled means reshaped, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A news piece is rewritten in a striking style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telling' looks like an adjective for effective, but it is the noun: a narration.
explanation.definitionFit: A detailed account or narration of facts, the act of recounting, is a recital.

clue.text: Blaze away, say, as pioneers do make one

definitions.text: Blaze away, say, as pioneers do make one

blocks.note: surface reading: firing guns freely, as frontier settlers might
setter's reading: pioneers blaze and make a path through new country

explanation.surface: Pioneers shooting off their guns on the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: To blaze a path is to mark it by notching trees; 'blaze away' here is not shooting.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough track or path through wild country is what explorers cut and mark.

clue.text: Being at home, if I marry, is so dull

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
an is an archaic word for if, as in Shakespeare
taken as written
to mate is to pair up or wed

explanation.surface: Someone fears domestic married life would be boring.
explanation.walkthrough: AN for 'if' is old usage, as in 'an it please you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifeless and without spirit, as if not alive at all; flat and spiritless.

clue.text: Reade's ready

blocks.note: first meaning: a novel of 1863 by Charles Reade
second meaning: the ready is slang for available money in notes and coins

explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade was a Victorian novelist; 'the ready' is old slang for money to hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical coins and banknotes, money immediately available, are what the slang word names; also the title of the Victorian novel.

clue.text: Hat-girl as artist's model

blocks.note: first meaning: a soft felt hat with a dented crown
second meaning: the heroine of George du Maurier's novel, who sits for painters in Paris

explanation.surface: A girl posing for a painter in a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: The felt hat took its name from the stage version of du Maurier's 1894 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft felt headgear named after the novel's heroine, who modelled for painters in Paris.
